# Automating the Analysis: Make and targets {#sec-pipelines}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Avoid Manual Data Manipulation Steps.*

[Sandve, Nekrutenko, Taylor, and Hovig]{.smallcaps}, *Ten
Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research*,
Rule 2 (2013)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

This chapter concerns the multi-step analysis that
someone runs by hand, script after script. By its end you
will be able to replace the running of such an analysis
with a single command whose completeness does not depend
on anyone's memory. That command rests on a dependency
graph that a tool, not an analyst, walks to decide what
has gone stale and what has not.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Loads the shared stack-diagram function so the fig-alt option
# below computes its text from the same call that draws the
# figure, rather than risk the two drifting apart.
pkgload::load_all('../..', quiet = TRUE)
```

## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 55 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** The determinant stack and the
capture-versus-validation distinction of Chapter 3
(@sec-levels). This chapter's central claim, that a
pipeline validates re-execution without capturing any new
layer, is stated entirely in those terms. The sealed,
reproducible render of Chapter 9 (@sec-literate). A
pipeline is what a growing analysis needs once some of
its computation has moved out of that single document and
into scripts. Comfort writing an R function with explicit
arguments and a return value, reading a short shell
command, and no prior exposure to Make, `targets`, or any
other build tool. In the one-quarter core path (see the
[Conventions](conventions.qmd) page), only the Make
section below is core. The `targets`, Snakemake,
Nextflow, and `workflowr` sections that follow it are
marked optional, and they can be skipped on that schedule
without losing the chapter's central claim.

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to
answer:**

- Can you diagnose the failure mode of a manually run,
  multi-step analysis: steps run out of order, an
  upstream change leaves a downstream output stale, and
  no one can be sure the whole thing still runs end to
  end from raw data to report?
- Can you express an analysis as a directed acyclic
  graph of steps, and explain why a single command can
  then rebuild exactly what is out of date and nothing
  more?
- Can you read and write a GNU Make rule, its target,
  prerequisites, and recipe, explain the timestamp-based
  staleness check, and say why Make's reach is
  language-agnostic?
- Can you build an R-native, function-oriented pipeline
  with `targets`, including `_targets.R`, `tar_target()`,
  `tar_make()`, and `tar_visnetwork()`, and explain how
  `targets` invalidates exactly the targets that depend on
  a changed function, object, or package?
- Can you state, in the book's capture-versus-validation
  terms, precisely what a pipeline does and does not add
  to the reproducibility ladder, and judge how heavily the
  pipeline machinery bears on each research archetype?

**Outline.**

- Where this sits on the stack: a pipeline validates, it
  does not capture.
- Orientation: a report stale behind a corrected dataset.
- The analyst's contribution: granularity, honest
  dependency declarations, and the level a pipeline does
  not establish.
- The analysis as a dependency graph: the DAG, and its
  cost measured rather than asserted.
- GNU Make: targets, prerequisites, rules, and the
  timestamp check.
- `targets`: a function-oriented pipeline that hashes code
  and objects, not just file times.
- What a pipeline does, and does not, add to the ladder.
- Pipelines across the archetypes.
- Beyond R: Snakemake, Nextflow, and `workflowr`.
- Worked example: refactoring four scripts into a
  `targets` pipeline.
- The cohort, continued: the compendium's own two-step
  graph, timed.
- A language model inside the pipeline: a dependency no
  rung pins, and its responses kept as data.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: from earlier chapters

A collaborator updates `survival` to a newer release and
commits the new `renv.lock`. You pull the commit, run
`renv::restore()`, and render the whole Quarto project, whose
`_quarto.yml` sets `freeze: auto`. The hazard ratio on the
page is unchanged, under a fresh build date. Drawing on
@sec-dependencies and @sec-literate, which determinant
layer changed, can the page tell you whether the new
release moved the estimate, and what render would?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The layer that changed after the `survival` update is the
package-versions layer. The new `renv.lock` records the
newer release, and `renv::restore()` reinstalls exactly
the versions the lockfile records (@sec-dependencies). The
page cannot tell you whether the estimate moved. Under
`freeze: auto`, a project render compares only with the
document's own source, so an updated package leaves the
frozen results in `_freeze/` in place under a fresh build
date (@sec-freeze). Rendering that single document always
executes its code. For a deposited analysis, render in the
pinned environment with freeze off, or after deleting
`_freeze/` and the cache directories (@sec-literate).
:::
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

We begin by locating the chapter on the determinant
stack. Its claim is the sharpest negative result in the
book so far: the pipeline tools it teaches pin no new
determinant at all. They do not fix a package version,
and they do not fix an operating system or an R runtime;
that is the work of @sec-dependencies and @sec-containers.
What a pipeline does is confirm, mechanically and on every
run, that the recorded analysis code and the input data
currently in hand are the ones a given output reflects.
We therefore mark, in @fig-stack-pipelines, the
analysis-code and input-data layers as validated here, not
captured. This is the same reading @sec-testing gives its
own test suite for the same two layers, though by a
different mechanism: a test suite checks that the code is
*correct* on some input, where a pipeline checks only
that an output is *current* with respect to whatever input
it was last given, correct or not.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stack-pipelines
#| fig-cap: 'The determinant stack of @sec-levels, with the analysis-code and input-data layers marked as validated, not captured, by a pipeline tool. Make and `targets` confirm that a recorded output is current with respect to the code and data that produced it; they do not pin a package version, an operating system, or an R runtime, and they say nothing about whether the code or the data are correct, only whether the output in hand still reflects them.'
#| fig-alt: !expr determinant_stack_alt(validates = c('Analysis code', 'Input data'))
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
plot_determinant_stack(
  validates = c('Analysis code', 'Input data'),
  title = 'A pipeline validates currency; it captures no layer')
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: capture or validation, again

A colleague argues that adding a `_targets.R` pipeline to
a project must raise its reproducibility level, since the
project can now be rebuilt with one command instead of
several remembered ones. Using this chapter's stack
figure, is the colleague correct?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The pipeline pins no layer of the determinant stack:
the package versions, the operating system, and the R
runtime are exactly as pinned, or as unpinned, after
`_targets.R` is added as before. What changed is that the
analysis-code and input-data layers are now checked for
currency on every run rather than trusted to memory. That
is a validation feature, like continuous integration or a
baseline test, and it leaves the project's rung on the L0
to L3 ladder exactly where it was.
:::
:::

## Orientation

Consider an analysis that has grown, as most do, one
step at a time. There is a script that reads the raw
export and writes a cleaned dataset. A second fits
a model to the cleaned data and saves the fitted object.
A third draws the figures from the model, and a
report assembles the figures and the tables into a
manuscript. Each script runs, and the analyst runs them
in order, by hand, at the console. For a while this
works.

The trouble begins when the raw data are corrected. The
analyst re-runs the cleaning script, and now must
remember three further things. The model depends on the
cleaned data and must be re-run; the figures depend on
the model and must be re-run; and the report depends on
the figures and must be re-rendered. Each of these is a
separate act of memory. Miss one, and the report now
shows a figure drawn from the old model, fitted to the
old data, and nothing in the document announces the
discrepancy. The output is stale: it is downstream of a
change that never propagated to it. Worse, the staleness
is invisible, because a stale figure is a perfectly
valid PNG file that opens and displays without complaint.

This is the failure this chapter exists to prevent, and
it has three faces. The first is **order**. The steps
have a required sequence, cleaning before modeling
before plotting, and running them out of order produces
either an error or, more dangerously, a result computed
from the wrong inputs. The second is **staleness**. A
change to an upstream file leaves every downstream output
obsolete, and re-propagating the change by hand is
exactly the kind of bookkeeping a human does poorly. The
third is the **end-to-end doubt**. After a session of
editing scripts and re-running some of them, the analyst
cannot honestly say whether the whole analysis still runs
from raw data to finished report. It has been
weeks since anyone ran it all, in order, in one act. The
project works, in the sense that its outputs exist, but
no one can be sure it would work if rebuilt from nothing.

How, then, are we to remove memory from the process? The
remedy is to stop treating the analysis as a remembered
sequence of commands and to express it instead as a
structure. That structure is a graph of steps, each
declaring what it consumes and what it produces. From it
a machine can work out the order, detect the staleness,
and re-run exactly what a change requires. Such a
structure is a pipeline, and this chapter is about two
tools that build one, the venerable and language-agnostic
GNU Make and the R-native `targets`. The manual-steps
critique that motivates them is stated crisply in the
practices literature. @sandve2013, in their second rule,
urge that one 'avoid manual data manipulation steps' and
automate the path from raw data to result. Their reason
is that a manual path cannot be trusted to have been
followed the same way twice.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: naming the failure

An analyst corrects a typo in the raw data, re-runs the
modeling script because that is the step they are
thinking about, and ships the resulting report. The
figures were drawn from the model fitted before the
correction. Which of the orientation's three faces, order,
staleness, or end-to-end doubt, does this failure
illustrate, and why does the stale figure give no warning?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It is staleness. The correction to the raw data left the
figures, which depend on the model fitted from the old
data, out of date. Re-running only the modeling script did
not propagate the change the one additional step further.
The stale figure gives no warning because a stale PNG is a
perfectly valid image file. Nothing about its bytes
records what it was computed from, so neither the file
system nor a glance at the document can distinguish it
from a current one.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Three judgments in this chapter are the analyst's own,
and no pipeline tool makes them.

1. **Deciding where the steps divide.** A pipeline is a
   graph of steps, and the analyst chooses what a step is.
   That is, the analyst decides how finely to cut the
   analysis into targets, which computations to group and
   which to separate. Cut too
   coarsely, into one enormous step, and the pipeline
   caches nothing useful, because any change re-runs
   everything. Cut too finely, into hundreds of trivial
   targets, and the graph becomes hard to read and the
   bookkeeping overhead dominates. The right granularity
   puts the expensive, stable computations, a model fit, a
   simulation run, in targets of their own, so that a
   change elsewhere does not needlessly re-run them. The
   choice trades caching benefit against graph legibility.

2. **Keeping the dependency declarations honest.** A
   pipeline can only track dependencies it is told about,
   or can infer. Make infers nothing. Every prerequisite an
   analyst omits from a rule is a dependency the tool
   cannot see, and an omitted prerequisite is exactly how a
   stale output slips through. `targets` infers a great
   deal automatically, but it too can be defeated, by a
   step that reads a file without declaring it as a file
   target, or that reaches for global state the tool
   cannot trace. Getting the declared dependencies to match the
   real ones is the analyst's responsibility, and a
   pipeline's correctness rests on it.

3. **Matching the claim to what a pipeline delivers.** A
   pipeline mechanizes re-execution. It does not pin a
   package, fix an environment, or establish that a result
   is correct. An analyst who says 'the analysis is
   reproducible' because `tar_make()` runs to completion
   has claimed more than the pipeline delivers. This is
   the same overreach, for the same reasons, as treating
   the sealed render of @sec-literate as a
   reproducibility guarantee.
   The pipeline secures the act of re-running. The level
   reached is a separate question, settled by the
   lockfile, the container, and the verification of the
   later chapters.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: whose judgment, again

A `targets` pipeline runs green, end to end, on the
analyst's machine. Which of the three judgments above, if
any, has the green run settled, and which remain open?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A green run settles none of the three. It says nothing
about whether the targets were cut at a sensible
granularity, since a pipeline with one enormous target can
run green and still cache nothing useful. It says nothing
about whether the declared dependencies are complete,
since an undeclared input simply never triggers a rebuild
and the run stays green regardless. And it says nothing
about the level reached, since re-execution and pinning
are different questions entirely.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Pipeline.** An analysis expressed as a set of steps,
  each declaring its inputs and outputs, so that the whole
  can be re-executed by a single command that runs the
  steps in dependency order.
- **Dependency graph.** The graph whose nodes are the
  steps and whose edges record that one step consumes what
  another produces. A valid pipeline's graph is a
  *directed acyclic graph* (DAG): directed because inputs
  flow to outputs, and acyclic because a step cannot,
  directly or transitively, depend on its own output.
- **Target.** A single step in the pipeline, together with
  the output it produces. The word is shared by Make and
  `targets`, with a shift of emphasis: for Make a target is
  a file, for `targets` it is more often an R object.
- **Prerequisite.** In Make, an input a target depends on.
  If any prerequisite is newer than the target, the target
  is out of date.
- **Recipe (or command).** The shell command Make runs to
  bring a target up to date from its prerequisites.
- **Staleness (out-of-date).** The condition of a target
  whose inputs have changed since it was last built, so
  that its stored output no longer reflects its inputs.
- **Up-to-date (skippable).** The condition of a target
  whose inputs have not changed since it was last built, so
  that rebuilding it would reproduce the stored output and
  can be skipped.
- **Invalidation.** The act of marking a target out of
  date because something it depends on, a file, an upstream
  target, a function, or a package, has changed.
:::

## The analysis as a dependency graph

Having named the failure, we now turn to the structure
that prevents it. The conceptual move that a pipeline asks
of an analyst is to stop thinking of the analysis as a
list of commands to run. Instead, the analyst thinks of it
as a graph of dependencies to satisfy. The two
descriptions contain the same steps, but they license
different machinery. A list of commands can only be
replayed, from the top, every time. A graph of
dependencies can be interrogated, so that a tool can
answer the question a list cannot: which steps actually
need to run now, given what has changed?

@fig-pipeline-dag draws the graph for the small analysis
of the orientation. Each node is a step that produces an
output, and each arrow records that the step at its head
consumes what the step at its tail produces. The graph is
directed, because the flow from raw data to report has a
direction, and it is acyclic, because no output feeds,
however remotely, back into its own inputs. This is the
directed acyclic graph, the DAG, that every pipeline tool
builds internally, whether or not it draws it for the
reader.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pipeline-dag
#| fig-cap: 'The analysis of the orientation as a directed acyclic graph. Each node is a step that produces an output; each arrow records that the step it points to consumes what the previous step produced. A change to the raw data invalidates every node downstream of it (all four to its right); a change to the plotting code invalidates only the figures and the report. A pipeline tool reads this graph to rebuild exactly the stale nodes and skip the rest.'
#| fig-alt: 'Five labeled nodes in a single horizontal row, connected left to right by arrows: raw data, then cleaned data, then model, then figures, then report. Each arrow points from a step to the step that consumes its output, so the chain runs in one direction with no branches and no cycles.'
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.2

library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

nodes <- tibble(
  step = c('raw\ndata', 'cleaned\ndata', 'model',
           'figures', 'report'),
  x = 1:5,
  y = 0
)

edges <- tibble(
  x = 1:4,
  xend = 2:5,
  y = 0,
  yend = 0
)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = edges,
    aes(x = x + 0.30, xend = xend - 0.30,
        y = y, yend = yend),
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.16, 'cm'),
                        type = 'closed'),
    linewidth = 0.5, colour = 'grey45'
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = nodes,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = step),
    size = 3, lineheight = 0.9,
    label.padding = grid::unit(0.35, 'lines'),
    label.r = grid::unit(0.12, 'lines'),
    fill = 'grey96', colour = 'grey15'
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 5.5),
                  ylim = c(-1, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void()
```

Two operations on this graph are the whole point of a
pipeline. The first is the **topological sort**. Reading
the arrows, the tool can order the steps so that no step
runs before the steps it depends on. This is the order
the analyst was keeping in their head and now need not.
The second is **selective rebuild**. Given a record of
what each step last consumed, the tool can mark a step
stale when any of its inputs has changed and up to date
otherwise. It then rebuilds only the stale steps and
those downstream of them. If the raw data change, all
four downstream nodes are stale and all four rebuild. If
only the plotting code changes, the figures and the
report are stale but the cleaned data and the model are
not. The model, which may have taken an hour to fit, is
not re-fitted. The single command that triggers this,
`make` or `tar_make()`, replaces the remembered sequence
with one reliable act. The end-to-end doubt of the
orientation is thereby dissolved, because the one act, by
construction, runs everything that is out of date and
leaves nothing behind.

### The graph of an actual analysis

@fig-pipeline-dag draws the shape in the abstract. But
what does the shape cost over an analysis that actually
runs? There the same shape is less tidy than the diagram,
and the argument below depends on that untidiness.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pipeline-steps
#| tbl-cap: 'The retinopathy analysis expressed as a dependency graph, with the cost of each step measured rather than asserted. The timings are from one run on one machine and will differ on another, and repeated runs on the same machine have varied by several-fold; even the ratios between steps should be read as illustrative, not as a stable property of the analysis. Note that the expensive step sits at the end, so an edit to the plotting code that forced a full rebuild would waste almost all of the total.'

library(tibble)
library(knitr)

time_it <- function(expr) {
  t <- system.time(force(expr))[['elapsed']]
  round(1000 * t, 1)
}

d <- survival::diabetic
t_load <- time_it(d <- survival::diabetic)
t_clean <- time_it({
  d$arm <- factor(d$trt, levels = c(0, 1),
                  labels = c('Untreated', 'Laser'))
  d <- d[!is.na(d$time), ]
})
t_fit <- time_it(
  fit <- survival::coxph(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ arm + age,
                         data = d)
)
t_boot <- time_it({
  set.seed(1)
  replicate(200, {
    i <- sample(nrow(d), replace = TRUE)
    unname(coef(survival::coxph(
      survival::Surv(time, status) ~ arm + age, data = d[i, ]))[1])
  })
})

steps <- tibble(
  Step = c('read raw data', 'derive arm labels',
           'fit proportional-hazards model',
           'bootstrap the treatment effect'),
  `Consumes` = c('--', 'raw data', 'cleaned data',
                 'cleaned data'),
  `Elapsed (ms)` = c(t_load, t_clean, t_fit, t_boot)
)

kable(steps, align = 'llr')
```

```{r}
#| label: pipeline-steps-prose
#| include: false
t_total <- t_load + t_clean + t_fit + t_boot
boot_share <- floor(100 * t_boot / t_total)
```

On this build the bootstrap took `r t_boot` milliseconds,
at least `r boot_share` percent of the four steps' total,
and none of the other three took more than
`r max(t_load, t_clean, t_fit)` milliseconds. An analyst who re-runs everything after changing a
label pays for the bootstrap to learn nothing. Every
figure in these two paragraphs is an inline expression,
for the reason @sec-literate gives: had they been typed,
the next machine to build the book would have made them
false.

The table also carries a caveat about itself. These
timings are computed when the book is built, so they
describe the build machine and not the reader's. A slower
machine would show different absolute values, and so can
a second run on the same machine. Even the ratio of the
bootstrap to the model fit is unstable. The fit took
`r t_fit` milliseconds on this build, a quantity so small
that a millisecond or two of timer noise in that
denominator moves the ratio several-fold from one run to
the next. What held in every
repeated run is the ordering: the bootstrap dominates the
total, and the steps before it are negligible. That
ordering, not any single number, is what the table
supports. This is the same distinction the verification
chapter draws between a result worth recording and a
measurement worth repeating.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: reading the measured costs

@tbl-pipeline-steps shows the bootstrap taking almost all
of the total time. An analyst who changes only the color
of a figure, then reruns the whole four-step chain by
hand, without a pipeline, pays for which step
unnecessarily? And which feature of the table should be
expected to survive a change of machine?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The analyst pays for the bootstrap, the most expensive
step, even though a color change touches nothing the
bootstrap consumes; a selective rebuild would skip it
entirely. The absolute timings are properties of the one
machine that happened to build this chapter. They will
differ, often by a large factor, on another machine or
even on a repeated run of the same one. The ratio of the
bootstrap to the fit is not stable either, because the
fit's few milliseconds sit near the timer's resolution.
What survives is the ordering: the bootstrap is by far
the largest step, and it takes nearly all of the total.
The table is read for which step dominates, not for any
one number.
:::
:::

## GNU Make: targets, prerequisites, and rules

We turn now from the idea to the tools. The oldest and
most widely used pipeline tool is GNU Make, a
reimplementation of the `make` utility first written in
1976 to compile programs. It has been
pressed into service for data analysis ever since. Make
is worth learning first, before any R-specific tool, for
two reasons. First, its model is the simplest possible
expression of the pipeline idea, so that understanding it
is understanding pipelines in general. Second, its reach
is language-agnostic. A single Makefile can orchestrate
an analysis whose steps are written in R, Python, the
shell, and a typesetting engine, without knowing or
caring what language each step uses.

A Makefile is a list of **rules**, and a rule has three
parts. The first is a **target**, the file the rule
produces. The second is its **prerequisites**, the files
the target depends on, written after a colon. The third
is a **recipe**, the shell command that builds the target
from its prerequisites. The recipe is written on the
following line and, by an unforgiving convention,
indented with a literal tab.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

A text editor set to insert spaces for indentation will
silently turn that leading tab into spaces, and what Make
says then depends on the line. To see it, take the
four-rule Makefile below and replace the tab before
`Rscript make_figures.R` with eight spaces. GNU Make
stops with `Makefile:5: *** missing separator (did you
mean TAB instead of 8 spaces?).  Stop.` With four spaces
the hint disappears, and the bare 'missing separator'
names a line but not the cause. A spaced recipe that
contains a colon, such as the `rmarkdown::render()` line
of the first rule, raises no error at all. Make reads it
as one more rule, and `report.html` is left with no
recipe. For a permanent fix, configure the editor to
preserve a literal tab inside files named `Makefile`.
:::

The analysis of
@fig-pipeline-dag becomes four rules:

```makefile
report.html: report.Rmd figures.rds
	Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd")'

figures.rds: make_figures.R model.rds
	Rscript make_figures.R

model.rds: fit_model.R cleaned.rds
	Rscript fit_model.R

cleaned.rds: clean_data.R raw_data.csv
	Rscript clean_data.R
```

If we read the rules from the bottom up, the dependency
graph is plain. `cleaned.rds` depends on the cleaning
script and the raw data; `model.rds` depends on the
fitting script and the cleaned data; and so on up to the
report. Make never has to be told the order, because the
order is implied by the prerequisites. It reads the whole
Makefile, builds the graph, sorts it, and knows that
`cleaned.rds` must be built before `model.rds` because
the latter names the former as a prerequisite. To rebuild
the analysis the analyst types a single command:

```bash
make report.html
```

or, since the first target in the file is the default,
simply `make`. Make walks the graph and rebuilds what is
needed, in order, and reports each recipe as it runs.

But how does Make decide what is needed? The mechanism is
the one subtlety worth dwelling on, because it is both the
source of Make's power and the source of its most common
surprise. Make is **timestamp-based**. It compares the
modification time of each target against the modification
times of its prerequisites. It considers a target out of
date if any prerequisite is newer than the target.
Suppose we edit `fit_model.R`; its modification time
advances past that of `model.rds`. Make sees that
`model.rds` is now older than a file it depends on and
rebuilds it. That rebuild advances the timestamp of
`model.rds` past that of `figures.rds`, and so the
rebuild propagates downstream exactly as far as the
change reaches and no further. A target all of whose
prerequisites are older than it is already up to date.
Make skips it, printing a line to the effect that there
is nothing to be done. This is the selective rebuild of
the previous section, implemented with nothing more than
the file system's clock.

The timestamp rule is also Make's principal limitation. Make knows only whether a file is
newer, not whether its contents have changed. Touching a
file without editing it will trigger a needless rebuild.
More subtly, a change that does not alter a file's
modification time will be missed. Make also tracks only
what the analyst declares. It has no way to know that
`fit_model.R` reads a configuration file unless that file
is listed as a prerequisite. An undeclared input is
invisible, and its change will not trigger the rebuild it
should. Finally, Make tracks files and only files. It
cannot cache an in-memory R object, so every step must
serialize its result to disk, and the graph is a graph of
files. These limitations are the opening that the
R-native tools were built to close.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what Make rebuilds

A project uses the four-rule Makefile above. The analyst
edits `make_figures.R` to change a color palette and
runs `make`. Which of the four targets does Make rebuild,
and which does it skip? Explain your answer in terms of
the timestamp rule.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Editing `make_figures.R` advances its modification time
past that of `figures.rds`, so `figures.rds` is now older
than one of its prerequisites and Make rebuilds it.
Rebuilding `figures.rds` advances its timestamp past that
of `report.html`, so `report.html` is rebuilt too. Make
skips `cleaned.rds` and `model.rds`. Neither the raw data,
the cleaning script, the fitting script, nor the cleaned
data changed. Each of those targets therefore remains
newer than all of its prerequisites and is up to date. The expensive
model fit is not repeated.
:::
:::

## targets: a function-oriented pipeline for R

Make treats an analysis as a graph of files built by
shell commands. For an R analysis this is a slightly
awkward fit. Every step must be a script that reads files
and writes files, and the intermediate objects must all
be serialized to disk by hand. Moreover, Make's timestamp
check is blind to the thing an R analyst most wants
tracked, the R functions that do the work. The `targets`
package, written by William Landau as the successor to
his earlier `drake` [@landau2018; @landau2021], reworks
the pipeline idea natively for R. It closes exactly these
gaps.

The reframing is captured in the phrase
'function-oriented'. In a `targets` pipeline the analyst
writes the analysis as a set of R functions, one for each
meaningful step. The analyst then declares a list of
targets that connect those functions into a graph, in a
special script named `_targets.R` at the project root.
Each target is created by `tar_target()`, which names the
target and gives the R expression that produces it.
The package reads those expressions and notices that one
target's expression mentions another target's name. From
this it infers the dependency graph automatically, with
no colons and no prerequisites to maintain by hand. A
`_targets.R` for our running analysis reads:

```r
library(targets)
library(tarchetypes)
tar_option_set(packages = c('dplyr', 'ggplot2'))

# Analysis functions live in R/ and are sourced here.
tar_source('R')

list(
  tar_target(
    raw_file,
    'data/raw_data.csv',
    format = 'file'
  ),
  tar_target(raw_data, read_raw(raw_file)),
  tar_target(cleaned, clean_data(raw_data)),
  tar_target(model, fit_model(cleaned)),
  tar_target(figures, make_figures(model, cleaned)),
  tar_render(report, 'report.Rmd')
)
```

The last line needs a word, because it is where a
hand-written pipeline most often goes wrong. A report is a
file produced from another file, the `report.Rmd` source.
The target that renders it must therefore track that
source as well as the results it displays.
`tar_render()`, from the companion package `tarchetypes`,
does both. It tracks `report.Rmd` as a file, and it reads
the document for calls such as `tar_read(model)` and
`tar_load(figures)`, making each target so named a
dependency of the report. Inside `report.Rmd`, results are
therefore fetched with `targets::tar_read()` rather than
recomputed. For a Quarto document, `tar_quarto()` plays
the same role. The tempting alternative is a plain
`tar_target(report, render_report(model,
figures), format = 'file')`. It tracks the model, the
figures, and the rendered HTML, but not the source. In a
scratch run with `targets` 1.12.0 and `tarchetypes`
0.14.0, editing the report's prose left `tar_outdated()`
empty under that pattern, while under `tar_render()` it
listed `report`. A report that does not rebuild when its
own text changes is a stale report that the pipeline
calls current.

Several features distinguish this from the Makefile. The
intermediate results, `raw_data`,
`cleaned`, `model`, `figures`, are **R objects, not
files**. `targets` stores each in a hidden `_targets/`
store, keyed and versioned, and hands it to the next
target as a plain R value. The analyst never writes a
`saveRDS` or a `readRDS`, because the storage is the
tool's job. Where a real file must be tracked, such as the
raw CSV at the top, the target is declared with
`format = 'file'`. `targets` then watches the file's
contents, by hashing them, rather than the R object.
`tar_render()` does the same for the report's source and
its rendered output.

That hashing is the second and deeper difference. Where
Make compares timestamps, `targets` compares **content
hashes**, so that a file touched but not changed does not
trigger a rebuild. The hashing is not unconditional,
however. When the `trust_timestamps` option is left
unset, `targets` chooses by file system. On a file system
with precise time stamps it trusts them: it compares a
tracked file's modification time with the one
it recorded and recomputes the hash only if the two
differ. A file whose content changed while its time stamp
did not is therefore *not* caught. Such changes are rare
in ordinary editing, but copying tools that preserve time
stamps, and file systems with coarse time stamps, can
produce them. In a scratch run with `targets` 1.12.0, a
one-digit edit to the raw CSV with its time stamp
restored left `tar_outdated()` empty under the default.
Under `tar_option_set(trust_timestamps = FALSE)`, by
contrast, it listed every target downstream of the file,
at the cost of hashing every tracked file on every check.

The hashing also extends past the data to the code.
`targets` records a hash of the body of every function a
target calls, and of the R expression in the target
itself. Editing `fit_model()` therefore invalidates the
`model` target, and everything downstream of it, even
though no file has changed at all. Make, seeing only
files, cannot detect such a change. A changed function
invalidates exactly the targets that use it, directly or
transitively, and no others. A change to `make_figures()`
invalidates `figures` and `report` but leaves `model`
untouched, and the expensive fit is preserved.
Sensitivity to the *versions* of the packages a target
loads is a separate matter, and one that `targets` does
not provide. `tar_option_set(packages =
...)` merely attaches those packages to each target's
evaluation environment, as a call to `library()` would.
By default `targets` does not track a package's version
or invalidate a target when that version changes.
Version-sensitivity comes from the lockfile of
@sec-dependencies, which is why Landau recommends using
`renv` alongside `targets`.

Two commands drive the pipeline. To see the graph,
`tar_visnetwork()` draws it as an interactive network,
coloring each target by whether it is up to date or out
of date. This is @fig-pipeline-dag made live and
queryable:

```r
tar_visnetwork()
```

To run the pipeline, `tar_make()` walks the graph, in a
fresh R session, and builds every target that is out of
date while **skipping every target that is up to date**:

```r
tar_make()
```

On the first run every target builds and `targets`
reports each in turn. If we edit `make_figures()` and run
`tar_make()` again, the output is eloquent. `targets`
names `figures` and `report` as built, and reports
`raw_data`, `cleaned`, and `model` as already current. In
`targets` 1.12 and later the up-to-date targets are
summarized as a count in the progress display rather than
listed by name. The distinction between what rebuilt and
what did not is unchanged. The analyst did not have to
remember which steps the edit affected; the tool derived
it from the graph and the hashes. A companion command,
`tar_outdated()`, answers the end-to-end doubt directly.
It lists the targets that a `tar_make()` would rebuild,
without running anything. One can thus ask, at any
moment, 'what is stale?' and get an exact answer.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Verification

To see this hold: in a project with `_targets.R`, run
`tar_make()` once, then edit the body of any function a
target calls, change nothing else, and run `tar_outdated()`
before rebuilding. It should name that target and every
target downstream of it, and no others. To make it fail on
purpose, add a line to a function that instead reads a file
directly with `read.csv()` rather than through a declared
`format = 'file'` target. Change that file's contents, and
run `tar_outdated()` again. The target that silently reads
the file will not appear, because `targets` cannot hash a
dependency it was never told about. This is the same
discipline failure Make suffers from an undeclared
prerequisite.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what `targets` tracks that Make does not

In the Makefile, editing the body of a function used by
`fit_model.R` without changing any file's dependency
declaration might not trigger a rebuild of the downstream
targets. Explain why `targets` does trigger it, and name
the two things `targets` hashes that Make does not.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Make decides staleness by comparing file modification
times against declared prerequisites, so a change that is
not reflected in a listed prerequisite's timestamp is
invisible to it. `targets` instead hashes the contents of
its inputs and also the bodies of the functions
each target calls and the R expression in the target
itself. Editing the function body changes its hash, which
invalidates every target that calls it and everything
downstream, so the rebuild propagates correctly. The two
things `targets` hashes that Make does not are the R
function definitions and the in-memory R objects (rather
than only on-disk files). Together these let it track
code changes and object changes that a timestamp
comparison cannot see.
:::
:::

## What a pipeline does, and does not, add

With both tools in hand, we may now ask what they have
bought us. What a pipeline contributes to reproducibility
is easily overstated in one direction and undersold in
the other. The book's capture-versus-validation framework
allows a precise statement.

Recall the framework. A computational result depends on a
stack of determinants: the operating system, the system
libraries, the R version, the package versions, the
session configuration, the data, the source.
Reproducibility is secured by *capturing* each
determinant, which is what a lockfile and a container do.
It is secured also by *validating* that the capture
suffices, which is what continuous integration and
verification do. The ladder, L0 locatable, L1 pinned
packages, L2 pinned environment, L3 verified, measures how
far down the stack an effort has reached.

Against this framework the pipeline occupies a precise and
initially surprising position: **a pipeline captures no
new determinant and adds no rung to the ladder.** It does
not pin a package version; that is the lockfile's work,
unchanged by whether a pipeline exists. It does not fix an
environment; that is the container's. It does not verify
that an output is correct; that is verification's. An
analysis run through `targets` and an identical analysis
run by hand, on the same machine, with the same packages,
produce the same numbers and sit at the same level of the
ladder.

Yet it would be wrong to conclude that the pipeline is
reproducibility-neutral. The reason returns us to the
distinction that organizes the book. What a pipeline does
is **mechanize the re-execution** that validation depends
on. Verification, in @sec-verification, checks that
rebuilding the analysis from its captured inputs
reproduces the recorded outputs; continuous integration
runs that rebuild on every change, in a clean machine.
Both presuppose that 'rebuild the analysis' is a single,
reliable, complete act. A manually run analysis cannot
guarantee precisely that act, because the human running it
may re-run some steps and forget others. The pipeline
turns 'rebuild the analysis' from a remembered sequence
into one command whose completeness is structural. In
doing so it removes the 'did I re-run everything?' doubt
that undermines every validation step. Like continuous
integration, a pipeline captures no determinant and adds
no rung; it makes the re-execution that verification
(@sec-verification) confirms reliable and repeatable.

The relation to continuous integration is especially
close, and worth making explicit, because the two are
sometimes confused. Continuous integration is the machine
that is not ours, running the rebuild in a clean
environment on every change. The pipeline is the
definition of what 'the rebuild' means. They compose
naturally. For a pipelined project, a CI workflow's core
step is to restore the environment and then run
`tar_make()` or `make`. The pipeline supplies the
re-execution, and CI supplies the clean, automatic,
external trigger for it. Neither replaces the other. The
pipeline without CI still requires a human to remember to
run it; CI without a pipeline must hard-code the sequence
of steps that the pipeline would have derived from the
graph. Together they close the loop. A change is pushed,
a clean machine rebuilds the analysis, and the result is
checked, with no act of memory anywhere in the chain. On
a clean runner the `_targets/` store is absent, because
it is not in the checkout, so the rebuild runs the whole
graph, which is itself the clean-rebuild test. A runner
rebuilds only what a change made stale when the store is
restored between runs, from a cache or a cloud store.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the composed claim

A team reports that 'every push rebuilds and tests the
analysis, so it is reproducible.' Using this section's
account of what CI and the pipeline each contribute, what
exactly has been shown, and what rung, if any, has been
demonstrated?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

What has been shown is that the pipeline's definition of
'rebuild' runs to completion on an external, clean machine
on every change, which is strong evidence of re-execution.
It is not, by itself, evidence of any rung. CI supplies
the clean trigger and the pipeline supplies the complete
recipe, but neither pins a package, fixes an environment,
or compares an output with a recorded baseline. The rung
actually reached depends entirely on whether a lockfile,
a container, and a baseline comparison also exist. 'It
runs on every push' answers a question about re-execution,
not about level.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own practice runs `tar_make()` and `make`
to completion on demand. That demonstrates re-execution
and nothing about the level actually reached. The level
is settled only by the lockfile, the container, and the
baseline comparison of the chapters this one does not
replace.
:::

## Pipelines across the archetypes

We turn next to how much of this machinery each kind of
project needs. The weight a pipeline tool carries varies
sharply across the research archetypes;
@tbl-archetype-weight in @sec-compendium is the reference.
It is most useful for the **data-analysis** archetype's
chain of transforms, run and re-run as the cleaning and
the model are adjusted. It is stronger still for a
**simulation study**. There `targets`' *branching*,
creating one target per parameter setting from a single
declaration, maps a whole parameter grid onto the
dependency graph, so adding a setting rebuilds only the
new cell. A **manuscript**'s pipeline is present but
modest and often implicit, since the sealed `report.Rmd`
of @sec-literate is itself a small, one-target build. The
sharpest contrast is the **R-package** archetype, which
has no analysis pipeline at all. A package is a library
of functions, not a chain of data transforms producing a
report, and its 're-execution' is `R CMD check`
(@sec-testing), not `tar_make()`. The **blog** archetype
returns to a pipeline, but over documents rather than an
analysis. Its natural rebuild touches only the posts whose
sources changed, the role `workflowr` fills in the next
section. Reach for the tool where re-execution is frequent
or costly, and do not impose its overhead where a single
render suffices.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: an archetype with no pipeline

A reader building an R package asks why this chapter never
shows a `_targets.R` for it. What is the answer, and what
plays the corresponding role?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A package has no chain of data transforms producing a
report, so there is no dependency graph of the kind a
pipeline tool rebuilds selectively. Its deliverable is a
library of functions, not a sequence of derived outputs.
`R CMD check`, together with the test suite, plays the
corresponding role. It determines what must be re-verified
given what changed and refuses to accept a stale result.
This is the same job a pipeline does for a data analysis,
performed by the package toolchain instead.
:::
:::

## Beyond R: Snakemake, Nextflow, and workflowr

Make and `targets` are the right tools for an R-centric
analysis. However, a reader whose work reaches beyond R, or
beyond a single machine, should know the tools that
dominate computational science more widely. In pipelines,
the R ecosystem is a small part of a much larger field.

The two dominant language-agnostic pipeline managers come
from bioinformatics. There, analyses routinely chain
dozens of command-line tools across terabytes of
sequencing data and must run at the scale of a computing
cluster or a cloud. **Snakemake**, by Köster and Rahmann,
extends the Make model, rules with inputs and outputs,
into a Python-based language. That language has pattern
rules, wildcards, and native awareness of cluster
schedulers, so that a single workflow definition can fan
a computation out across thousands of jobs [@koster2012].
**Nextflow**, by Di Tommaso and colleagues, takes a
different, dataflow approach, connecting processes
through channels. It is built from the ground up for
portability across high-performance-computing clusters and
cloud platforms, with containerization of each step as a
first-class feature [@ditommaso2017]. Both far exceed Make
and `targets` in their handling of scale and
heterogeneity. Both are the correct choice when an
analysis spans many languages and many machines. For a
first-year health-sciences analysis run on a laptop or a
single server in R, they are heavier than the problem
requires. A reader moving into genomics or large-scale
imaging, however, will meet them quickly and should
recognize them as the same pipeline idea scaled up.

Closer to home, **`workflowr`**, by Blischak and
colleagues, serves the specific case of a reproducible
research website [@blischak2019]. This covers the blog
archetype above and the versioned analysis site more
generally. Its contribution is less the pipeline than the
binding of each rendered result to version control.
`workflowr` rebuilds the documents that have changed and
stamps each rendered page with the git commit of the
source that produced it. Every published figure thus
carries, visibly, the version of the code behind it. It
is the natural tool where the deliverable is a website of
analyses that must each be traceable to a commit. It also
composes with the version-control discipline that runs
through this book.

The pipeline idea, express the analysis as a dependency
graph and rebuild only what is stale, is common to all
five tools. The choice among them is a choice of scale and
setting. Make is the language-agnostic minimum, and
`targets` is the R-native tool that tracks objects and
functions. Snakemake and Nextflow are the same idea at
cluster and cloud scale, and `workflowr` is the idea
applied to a versioned website. We now put the R-native
tool to work on a concrete case.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: choosing among the five tools

A genomics collaborator's analysis chains forty
command-line tools across a cluster, written in a mix of
Python and shell. Which of this section's tools fits, and
why would `targets` be the wrong reach here?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Snakemake or Nextflow fits. Both are built for exactly
this setting, many languages, many steps, and execution
spread across a cluster or the cloud, with native support
for job schedulers that Make and `targets` lack. `targets`
would be the wrong reach because it is R-native. Its
dependency inference works by hashing R function bodies
and R objects. That has nothing to track in a pipeline
whose steps are Python scripts and shell commands calling
external tools.
The pipeline idea is the same; the tool must match the
language and the scale.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To illustrate, we convert the running analysis from a set
of hand-run scripts into a `targets` pipeline, as a health
scientist tidying a working project would. The analysis
begins as four scripts in `analysis/scripts/`, run in
order at the console. One cleans `data/raw_data.csv` and
saves `cleaned.rds`, one fits a model and saves
`model.rds`, one draws figures, and one renders the
report. The project works, but every correction to the
raw data sets off the manual re-running the orientation
warned against.

The first step is to refactor the scripts into functions,
before any `_targets.R` is written, because a
function-oriented pipeline needs functions. Each script's
body becomes a function in `R/`: `read_raw()`,
`clean_data()`, `fit_model()`, and `make_figures()`. Each
takes its inputs as arguments and returns its result
rather than reading and writing files by side effect. The
fourth script, the report, becomes `report.Rmd`. It
fetches the model and the figures with
`targets::tar_read()` instead of recomputing them, so that
`tar_render()` can see what it depends on. This
refactoring is worthwhile on its own. Functions with
explicit inputs and outputs are testable in the sense of
@sec-testing, where a script that reads and writes global
files is not.

The second step is the `_targets.R` shown earlier in the
chapter. It declares the six targets: the raw file, the
read data, the cleaned data, the model, the figures, and
the report. It then lets `targets` infer the graph from
the way each target's expression names the targets before
it. With the file in place, `tar_visnetwork()` draws the
graph, and the analyst confirms it carries the intended
structure of @fig-pipeline-dag. Every node is initially
colored 'outdated' because nothing has been built yet.
@fig-pipeline-dag is a simplified linear schematic of the
chain from raw data to report. The actual dependency
graph is more connected. The `_targets.R` declares that
`figures` depends on both `model` and `cleaned` and that
`report` depends on both `model` and `figures`. Hence
`tar_visnetwork()` draws those extra cross-edges that the
schematic omits.

The third step is to build the pipeline once, with
`tar_make()`. This runs all six targets in dependency
order in a fresh session and populates the `_targets/`
store. A correction to the raw data, followed by
`tar_make()`, rebuilds all five downstream targets and
skips nothing, because everything depends on the data. A
refinement to `make_figures()`, followed by `tar_make()`,
rebuilds only `figures` and `report`. `raw_data`,
`cleaned`, and `model` are left untouched, the model fit,
the expensive step, among them. In current versions of
`targets` the console reports the untouched targets only
as a skip count. A change to the wording of the discussion
in `report.Rmd` rebuilds `report` alone. At any moment
`tar_outdated()` answers the question the manual workflow
could never answer with confidence. It lists precisely the
targets a rebuild would touch, so that the analyst always
knows whether the project is current.

The final step ties the pipeline to the validation
machinery of the surrounding chapters. The pipeline runs
inside the pinned environment of @sec-containers, restored
from the lockfile of @sec-dependencies. Thus `tar_make()`
re-executes against fixed packages and a fixed R. The
continuous-integration workflow of @sec-verification is
given one core instruction, to restore the environment and
run `tar_make()`. Every push then rebuilds the whole
pipeline on a clean machine, since the runner starts
without a `_targets/` store. The 'did I re-run
everything?' doubt is answered, permanently, by a machine
that is not the author's.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the two-target split

The worked example's `_targets.R` declares `raw_file` with
`format = 'file'` and a separate target `raw_data` that
reads it, rather than one target that both names the path
and reads it. Why does the split matter, and what would go
wrong without it?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

`format = 'file'` tells `targets` to hash whatever the
target's own return value points to. Only a target that
returns a path, such as the string `'data/raw_data.csv'`,
can carry that option. `read_raw(raw_file)` returns a data
frame, not a path. Declaring it `format = 'file'` would
make `targets` try to hash a data frame as though it were a
file path and fail. Splitting the tracked file from the
object read from it is what lets `targets` watch the raw
file's contents while still storing the loaded data frame
as an ordinary R object.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: complete the `_targets.R`

The worked example's `_targets.R`, first shown in the
section on `targets`, is reprinted here with four decisive
lines replaced by numbered placeholders. Write each missing
line, using only the functions and target names the worked
example defines.

```{.r}
library(targets)
library(tarchetypes)
tar_option_set(packages = c('dplyr', 'ggplot2'))

# Analysis functions live in R/ and are sourced here.
tar_source('R')

list(
  tar_target(
    raw_file,
    'data/raw_data.csv',
    # (1) ____: hash the file's contents, not an R object
  ),
  # (2) ____: read the raw file through its target name
  tar_target(cleaned, clean_data(raw_data)),
  tar_target(model, fit_model(cleaned)),
  # (3) ____: draw the figures from the model and the data
  # (4) ____: render report.Rmd, tracking its source
)
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The four missing lines of the worked example's
`_targets.R` are these.

(1) `format = 'file'`. It belongs on `raw_file` because
that target returns a path; on a target that returns a data
frame, `targets` would try to hash the data frame as a file
path and fail.

(2) `tar_target(raw_data, read_raw(raw_file)),`. Naming
`raw_file` in the expression is what declares the
dependency. A plausible `read_raw('data/raw_data.csv')`
reads the same file, but `targets` was never told about it
and cannot see a change to it.

(3) `tar_target(figures, make_figures(model, cleaned)),`.
Naming both targets draws the edges from `model` and from
`cleaned`; a figure function that fetched the data some
other way would hide the second edge from the graph.

(4) `tar_render(report, 'report.Rmd')`. The tempting
`tar_target(report, render_report(model, figures),
format = 'file')` tracks the model, the figures, and the
rendered HTML but not the source, so editing the report's
prose leaves `tar_outdated()` empty.
:::
:::

## The cohort, continued

This chapter has so far reasoned about pipelines through a
composite analysis. We now apply the same idea to this
book's own compendium. Here is a two-node graph, raw
extract to cleaned cohort, with the cost of each step
measured, as @tbl-pipeline-steps did for the retinopathy
example.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cohort-pipeline
#| tbl-cap: 'The two steps `load_cohort()` and `clean_cohort()` perform on the running cohort compendium, with elapsed time measured on one run on the machine that built this chapter; repeated runs vary and should not be read as a stable property of either function.'
cohort_path <- '../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'

t_load_cohort <- time_it(
  raw <- load_cohort(cohort_path))
t_clean_cohort <- time_it(
  cohort <- clean_cohort(raw))

cohort_steps <- tibble(
  Step = c('load_cohort()', 'clean_cohort()'),
  Consumes = c('cohort_raw.csv', 'the raw data frame'),
  `Elapsed (ms)` = c(t_load_cohort, t_clean_cohort),
  `Rows out` = c(nrow(raw), nrow(cohort))
)

kable(cohort_steps, align = 'llrr')
```

```{r}
#| label: cohort-rung
#| include: false
has_lock <- file.exists('../../renv.lock')
has_docker <- file.exists('../../Dockerfile')
cohort_rung <- if (has_lock && has_docker) {
  'L2'
} else if (has_lock) {
  'L1'
} else {
  'L0'
}
cohort_state <- c(
  'neither a lockfile nor a Dockerfile',
  'a lockfile but no Dockerfile',
  'a Dockerfile but no lockfile',
  'both a lockfile and a Dockerfile'
)[1 + has_lock + 2 * has_docker]
```

The two functions are already, in effect, a two-rule
pipeline. `clean_cohort()` consumes what `load_cohort()`
produces, and nothing downstream exists yet. No later
chapter's model or report has been wired to this extract
through `targets` or a Makefile. Suppose a correction were
made to `cohort_raw.csv` today, by hand. The only way to
know that `clean_cohort()`'s output had gone stale would
be to remember to re-run this cell. That is exactly the
end-to-end doubt the orientation opened with, now visited
on the book's own running example. Expressing this pair
as three targets would make that staleness mechanical
rather than remembered:

```r
list(
  tar_target(raw_file, cohort_path, format = 'file'),
  tar_target(raw, load_cohort(raw_file)),
  tar_target(cleaned, clean_cohort(raw))
)
```

The `raw_file` target is what makes `targets` watch the
CSV's contents. Without it, a lone
`tar_target(raw, load_cohort(cohort_path))` would track
only the value of the string `cohort_path`, and a
corrected CSV at the same path would leave `raw`
current. The cost is a three-target scaffold in the
pattern of the five-target one shown in Exercise 3's
solution below.
The repository holds `r cohort_state`, which places the
compendium at `r cohort_rung`. Adding the pipeline would
not move it off that rung, since a pipeline pins no
determinant. It would only make the one existing
transform trustworthy to rebuild without having to recall
that it exists.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the pipeline would, and would not, fix

Suppose the three-target pipeline above has been built
once, and `cohort_raw.csv` is then corrected. What would
`tar_outdated()` report, and would adding the pipeline
change the compendium's rung on the L0 to L3 ladder?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

`tar_outdated()` would report all three targets,
`raw_file`, `raw`, and `cleaned`, as out of date. The
file target `raw_file` hashes the corrected CSV's new
contents, `raw` depends on `raw_file`, and `cleaned`
depends on `raw`. No, the rung would not change.
The pipeline would still pin no package version, no R
runtime, and no operating system. The compendium would
therefore remain at `r cohort_rung`, the rung set by
what the repository holds (`r cohort_state`), whatever
`tar_outdated()` reports. The pipeline only guarantees
that a rebuild, once triggered, rebuilds the right
things.
:::
:::

## A language model inside the pipeline {#sec-llm-in-pipeline}

The rest of this chapter treats every step as code the
analyst controls. A step that sends text to a language
model is different in kind. Examples include coding
free-text clinical notes for smoking status and extracting
a variable from a radiology report. In the terms of
@sec-levels, the model is a dependency that no rung pins.
It runs remotely, under an identifier the provider can
update or retire, and it need not return the same output
twice for the same input. A lockfile cannot record it, and
a container cannot hold it.

The remedy is to treat the responses as data rather than
as computation. Four practices follow.

- **Cache responses as versioned derived data.** Store them
  in a committed file, one row per input, keyed by a hash
  of the input text, the prompt version, and the model
  identifier, and let the pipeline read that file. The
  `_targets/` store is not enough on its own, because it is
  absent from a fresh clone, and a rebuild there would
  query the model again.
- **Record the model and its settings.** Each row carries
  the model identifier the endpoint reported, the
  parameters sent, and the date of the query.
- **Version prompts as code.** A prompt is a file in the
  compendium, changed only by commit, and its hash enters
  the key.
- **Treat a re-query as a new measurement.** Responses
  obtained again, after a change of prompt or model or the
  loss of the originals, are a second rater's codes, not a
  re-execution. Report their agreement with the first set
  rather than presenting them as the same result.

The inputs fall under the restricted-data rule of the next
section before any query is made. Clinical notes are among
the most identifying records a study holds. The responses
derived from them inherit the notes' restrictions, which
decides where the cache may be deposited.

The fragment below is illustrative and abridged, and it is
not run. The query itself lives in a separate script that
the analyst runs by hand and whose new rows the analyst
reviews before committing. `tar_make()` never contacts the
endpoint: `join_responses()` matches each note to its row
and stops with a list of the missing keys rather than
filling them.

```r
# _targets.R (illustrative and abridged; not run)
library(targets)
tar_source('R')

list(
  tar_target(notes_file, 'analysis/data/raw_data/notes.csv',
             format = 'file'),
  tar_target(prompt_file, 'analysis/prompts/smoking-v2.txt',
             format = 'file'),
  tar_target(responses_file,
             'analysis/data/derived_data/smoking-responses.csv',
             format = 'file'),
  tar_target(notes, read_notes(notes_file)),
  tar_target(
    smoking,
    join_responses(notes, responses_file, prompt_file,
                   model_id = '<model identifier>')
  )
)
```

A clean rebuild then reproduces the coded data exactly.
The claim it supports is correspondingly narrow: the
analysis is reproducible given the committed responses,
not the model's coding of the notes.

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a fluent author of Makefiles and
`targets` pipelines. Its characteristic failures are worth
anticipating, because they bear directly on the one
discipline this chapter rests on, the honesty of the
dependency declarations.

{{< include _llm-rule.qmd >}}

For a pipeline, the structure to describe is the scripts,
the files each reads and writes, and the column names and
types of the data. A printed data frame or a log of
row-level output is derived output under the rule. A
coding agent asked to convert or run a pipeline will
execute it and so read every input it touches.

**Prompt.** 'Write a Makefile for my analysis: I have a cleaning
script, a modeling script, and a report.'

*Watch for.* The model cannot know the analyst's true
dependencies, so check every rule for a guessed one. Look
for an omitted prerequisite, such as a configuration file
the modeling script reads or a helper script the cleaning
script sources. Such a Makefile looks complete but fails
to rebuild when the undeclared input changes. Check also
for spaces where Make demands a literal tab to indent
recipes, a classic error that produces a 'missing
separator' message or, on a recipe line containing a
colon, no error at all.

*Verification.* Check every rule against what each step actually
reads and writes: list, for each script, its real inputs, and
confirm each appears as a prerequisite. The decisive test is
operational. Build once, then touch each declared input in
turn and confirm the expected targets rebuild. Then touch
an undeclared file the step secretly reads and confirm, as
a negative check, that the Makefile wrongly fails to
rebuild, which reveals the missing prerequisite.

**Prompt.** 'Convert my scripts to a `targets` pipeline.'

*Watch for.* Check for `format = 'file'` used incorrectly,
and for targets that read files directly inside the target
expression without declaring them as file targets.
`targets` then cannot see the dependency and will not
rebuild when the file changes. Check also that the scripts
were refactored into functions that return values, not
left as scripts called for their side effects, which
defeats the object-tracking that is the whole reason to
prefer `targets` over Make. Finally, check for a report
target that calls `rmarkdown::render()` inside a plain
`tar_target()`, which never tracks the report's source.

*Verification.* Confirm that every external file the pipeline
depends on is a `tar_target(..., format = 'file')` and that
intermediate results are returned R objects, not files written
by side effect. Then run `tar_make()`, edit one function body,
and confirm with `tar_outdated()` and a second `tar_make()` that
exactly the dependent targets, and no others, rebuild. Edit
one sentence of the report's prose and confirm that
`tar_outdated()` lists the report. If a
change to a function fails to invalidate a downstream target,
the dependency is not being tracked and the pipeline is lying
about what is current.

*A better prompt.* 'Convert the three attached scripts to a
`targets` pipeline. Their inputs and outputs are listed
below, with column names and types but no data. Refactor
each step into a function in `R/` that returns a value,
declare every file the pipeline reads as a
`format = 'file'` target, and render the report with
`tar_render()`. Then list, for each function, the targets
an edit to it should invalidate, so that I can check the
list against `tar_outdated()`.'

**Prompt.** 'Add a step to my pipeline that sends each
free-text note to `<tool name>` and codes it as current,
former, or never smoker.'

*Watch for.* Check where the call sits. A call inside a
target expression makes every rebuild of that target a
fresh query, so a corrected upstream file or a
`tar_destroy()` silently re-codes every note, unchanged
ones included, as a new measurement. Check also that the model identifier, the
parameters, and the prompt appear in committed files
rather than in the code's defaults.

*Verification.* Restructure the step as @sec-llm-in-pipeline
describes: responses in a committed file, keyed by input
hash, prompt, and model identifier, and a pipeline that
reads that file and never calls the endpoint. Then run
`tar_make()` from a fresh clone with the network disabled
and confirm that it completes. Before any note is sent,
apply the restricted-data rule above. If a coding agent
builds the step, the analyst runs the query script,
reviews the new responses, and commits them; an agent
that runs `tar_make()` or `tar_destroy()` should do so only
in a checkout where the real notes are not mounted
(@sec-llm-delegate).

## Exercises

1. Take a multi-step analysis of your own that you currently run
   by hand, and draw its dependency graph on paper: a node for
   each step, an arrow for each 'consumes the output of' relation.
   Confirm the graph is acyclic. Then identify, for a change to
   one upstream input of your choosing, exactly which nodes are
   downstream of it and would need to rebuild, and compare that
   set to the steps you would, in practice, remember to re-run by
   hand.

2. Write a Makefile of three or four rules for the analysis of
   the previous exercise. Run `make`, then edit one intermediate
   script and run `make` again, and record which targets rebuilt
   and which were skipped. Explain the result in terms of the
   timestamp rule. Then `touch` an input without changing its
   contents, run `make` once more, and explain why Make rebuilds
   a target whose contents did not change.

3. Convert the same analysis to a `targets` pipeline. Refactor
   each step into a function in `R/`, write `_targets.R`, and
   confirm with `tar_visnetwork()` that the graph matches the one
   you drew in exercise 1. Run `tar_make()`, then change the body
   of one function and, before rebuilding, predict with
   `tar_outdated()` which targets will rebuild. Run `tar_make()`
   and check your prediction.

4. Demonstrate the difference between Make's and `targets`'
   staleness checks. Choose a helper function that one of your
   scripts sources from a file the Makefile of exercise 2 does
   not list as a prerequisite. Edit its body in a way that
   changes the result, and confirm that `targets` invalidates
   the dependent targets. Explain, in one or two sentences, why
   the same edit could be missed by a Makefile that tracked
   only the script files' timestamps.

5. State, in the book's capture-versus-validation terms, what
   your pipeline has and has not added to the reproducibility of
   your project. Name the level on the ladder your project sits
   at, and identify what you would still need to do, a lockfile,
   a container, a verification against a baseline, to raise it,
   making explicit that none of those is supplied by the pipeline
   itself.

6. For each of the five archetypes, the data analysis, the
   simulation study, the manuscript, the R package, and the blog,
   write one or two sentences stating whether an analysis pipeline
   is central, modest, or absent, and why. For the archetype in
   which it is absent, name the mechanism that plays the
   corresponding role instead.

7. Run `cohort <- clean_cohort(load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'))`
   and report `nrow(cohort)`. Then write the three-target
   `_targets.R` fragment that wraps `load_cohort()` and
   `clean_cohort()` on this path, following the `raw_file`
   and `raw` split of Exercise 3's solution, and state what
   `tar_outdated()` would report immediately after the first
   `tar_make()` and after a second one with no file changed.

8. This exercise returns to the reproducibility ladder of
   Chapter 3 (@sec-levels). A project has a lockfile, a
   container, and a `targets` pipeline that runs green on
   every push, but no test compares a computed quantity with
   a value recorded earlier. State the single rung of the L0
   to L3 ladder this project occupies, and name the one
   artifact, absent here, whose addition would be needed to
   reach the next rung.

9. Take the illustrative `_targets.R` fragment of the
   section on a language model inside the pipeline
   (@sec-llm-in-pipeline). For each of four situations,
   state which targets `tar_outdated()` would list and what
   the next `tar_make()` would do: (a) a fresh clone, with
   the response file committed and no `_targets/` store;
   (b) a corrected spelling in one note; (c) a new version
   of the prompt file; (d) a new model identifier in
   `_targets.R`. Then say which situations call for a new
   query, and why its result is a new measurement rather
   than a re-execution.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. Every
exercise in this chapter is performed on an analysis of the
reader's own, so the outputs vary; the boxes record what
should happen and the reasoning that makes it expected.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
the gap between the downstream set and the remembered set.

On acyclicity: the graph must be acyclic because a cycle
would mean a step consumes, directly or indirectly, its own
output. There would then be no order in which to run the
steps. Readers occasionally draw what looks like a cycle
and find on inspection that they have drawn two different
versions of one file as a single node. Splitting the node
resolves it, and the resolution is itself informative,
since it names an artifact that is overwritten in place.

The instructive part is the comparison. The downstream set
of a change to a raw input is, in most analyses, everything:
cleaning, modeling, every figure, every table, the report.
The set most analysts re-run by hand is smaller, and it is
smaller in a characteristic way. People reliably re-run the
step they just edited and the thing they are looking at.
They reliably forget the intermediate results that nothing
on screen depends on, along with any figure that is not in
the document currently open.

The downstream set is a property of the graph, and a
person holding the graph in their head computes it
correctly only for small graphs and recent memory. A
pipeline tool computes it from the graph every time.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

Editing an intermediate script rebuilds that script's
target and everything downstream of it, and skips
everything upstream and everything on a parallel branch.
The timestamp rule explains it directly. Make rebuilds a
target whose modification time is older than any of its
declared prerequisites. Rebuilding a target advances its
own timestamp, so staleness propagates forward one link at
a time.

**Why `touch` triggers a rebuild.** Because Make does not
compare contents at all. It compares modification times,
and `touch` advances the modification time of the input
without changing a byte of it. Every target depending on
that input is now older than one of its prerequisites, so
Make rebuilds it, and the rebuild propagates downstream
exactly as a real edit would.

Make's guarantee is therefore conservative in one
direction and unreliable in the other. It will happily
rebuild things that did not need rebuilding, which costs
time and nothing else. It will also miss a change that
leaves timestamps as it found them, which costs
correctness. The first behavior is the one
this exercise demonstrates; the second is the subject of
exercise 4.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

The refactoring is the substance of the exercise. Each
Make rule becomes a function in `R/`, and `_targets.R`
declares the targets that call them:

```r
list(
  tar_target(
    raw_file,
    'data/raw_data.csv',
    format = 'file'
  ),
  tar_target(raw, read_raw(raw_file)),
  tar_target(cleaned, clean_data(raw)),
  tar_target(model, fit_model(cleaned)),
  tar_target(figures, make_figures(model, cleaned))
)
```

`format = 'file'` belongs on `raw_file`, not on `raw`: it
tells `targets` to hash the file at the path a target
returns, and only `raw_file` returns a path (the string
literal above). `raw` returns the data frame that
`read_raw()` builds from that path. Declaring it
`format = 'file'` therefore makes `targets` try to hash a
data frame as if it were a file path and error. The
two-target split, one target for the tracked file and one
for the object read from it, mirrors the pattern used
earlier in this chapter for the same reason.

`tar_visnetwork()` should show the same nodes and arrows
as the hand drawing. A mismatch is informative and usually
means the hand drawing missed a dependency, since
`targets` derives the graph from the code rather than from
memory.

On the prediction: after editing a function body,
`tar_outdated()` names that function's target and
everything downstream, and `tar_make()` rebuilds exactly
that set. Readers who predicted correctly have understood
the propagation rule; readers who predicted too small a
set usually forgot that invalidation is transitive.

The prediction is easy here and was hard in exercise 1,
on the same analysis, because `targets` made the graph
visible: the reader now reads the dependency structure
instead of recalling it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

Editing a function body in `R/` changes no file that a
Makefile would ordinarily list as a prerequisite of the
model target. The Makefile lists the *script* that fits
the model, not the helper file the script sources.
`targets` invalidates the dependent targets anyway, and
`tar_outdated()` names them before the rebuild.

**Why a Makefile could miss the equivalent edit.** Because
it tracks the timestamps of the files it was told to
track, and nothing told it about the helper. If
`fit_model.R` sources `R/helpers.R` and the rule declares
only `fit_model.R` as a prerequisite, then editing
`helpers.R` advances a timestamp Make never looks at.
Every downstream target remains, in Make's view, up to
date. The analysis then reports results computed by the
old function body, with no error and no indication that
anything is stale.

`targets` avoids this because it hashes the *bodies of the
functions each target calls*, and the R objects those
targets produce, rather than the modification times of a
declared file list. Because the dependency is discovered
from the code, the analyst cannot declare it incompletely.

The fair statement of the comparison is that a correctly
and completely written Makefile would catch this too. The
difference is that `targets` makes completeness the
default and Make makes it the analyst's responsibility,
and the failure mode of an incomplete Makefile is silence.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

**What the pipeline added.** In the book's terms, almost
nothing on the capture side and a good deal on the
validation side. The pipeline pins no layer of the
determinant stack: not the packages, not the environment,
not the R version. What it adds is a guarantee that the
outputs are *current with respect to the inputs*, which is
a form of internal consistency the analysis did not
previously have. It also adds an explicit, machine-readable
statement of the analysis structure, which is
documentation of a kind that cannot drift.

**The level.** The pipeline alone leaves the project where
it was, which for most readers is L0. This is the part of
the exercise most likely to be answered wrong, because a
`targets` pipeline feels like a large step forward and is,
on an axis the ladder does not grade.

**What would still be needed.** A lockfile to reach L1, a
container to reach L2, and verification against a recorded
baseline to reach L3. None of the three is supplied by the
pipeline, and the pipeline does not make any of them
easier or harder to add; they are orthogonal.

There is one honest qualification in the pipeline's favor.
Because it computes rather than remembers the downstream
