set, it removes a class of error, stale outputs, that
would otherwise defeat an L3 verification. Such a failure
would arise for reasons having nothing to do with the
environment. It does not
raise the level, and it makes the level easier to keep.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**Data analysis: central.** The archetype is a chain of
steps producing derived data and results, which is exactly
what a dependency graph describes.

**Simulation study: central.** Replicates are expensive
and independent, so recomputing only what is stale matters
more here than anywhere, and `targets` branching maps onto
the replicate structure directly.

**Manuscript: modest.** There is usually a pipeline behind
the manuscript, but the render itself is a single terminal
step and the literate document does much of the
orchestration. The pipeline earns its place when the
analysis feeding the document is expensive enough that
re-running it on every render is intolerable. That is the
same judgment the previous chapter framed as deciding what
the document computes at build time.

**Blog: modest to absent.** Each post is typically small
and self-contained, and the site generator already
rebuilds changed posts. A pipeline adds machinery for
little gain.

**R package: absent.** There is no chain of data
transformations to schedule; the deliverable is a set of
functions. **The mechanism that plays the corresponding
role is `R CMD check` together with the test suite**, which
performs the analogous job of determining what must be
re-verified and doing it. The analogy is closer than it
looks: both answer 'given what changed, what must be
recomputed', and both refuse to accept a stale result.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 7

The solution for this exercise is in the instructor
guide, which is distributed separately to course
instructors. Self-study
readers who want to check their answer can compare the
autogradable value and the `_targets.R` fragment against
those reported in the chapter's own 'The cohort,
continued' section.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 8

The project is at **L2, pinned environment**, and no
further. The lockfile and the container pin the packages
and the environment, and a `targets` pipeline that runs
green on every push demonstrates that the analysis
re-executes completely and reliably in that pinned
environment. None of this is a baseline comparison. A
green pipeline run shows that the code ran without error,
not that any reported quantity still matches a value
recorded earlier. This is exactly the L2-versus-L3
distinction Chapter 3 draws for a test suite with no
baseline test.

The missing artifact for L3 is a baseline test, a test that
recomputes a reported quantity and compares it with a value
committed to the repository within a stated tolerance.
Making the pipeline run the step that triggers that test
inside continuous integration, as @sec-verification
describes, is what turns the green run from a statement
about re-execution into evidence for L3. This chapter's
worked example stops short of that step: it has no
baseline test.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 9

In (a) there is no store, so every target is outdated.
`tar_make()` rebuilds them all from the committed files,
and `smoking` is reproduced exactly, because
`join_responses()` reads the committed responses and the
endpoint is never contacted. This is the case the design
exists for.

In (b) the hash of `notes_file` changes, so `notes` and
`smoking` are outdated. The corrected note has new text,
and therefore a new key with no row in the response file,
so `join_responses()` stops and names that one note. In
(c) the hash of `prompt_file` changes, so `smoking` is
outdated; because the prompt's hash enters every key,
every note is now missing and the stop names them all. In
(d) the command of `smoking` changes, which outdates it,
and again every key is missing.

Situation (a) needs no query. Situation (b) needs one
query, for the corrected note, and (c) and (d) need a
query for every note. You run those queries with the
separate script, review the new rows, and commit them
beside the old ones. Their result is a new measurement
because the model, as reached on a later date, need not
return what it returned before, even under an unchanged
identifier, and in (c) and (d) the instrument itself has
changed. Where old and new codes exist for the same note,
report their agreement, as you would for a second rater.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-pipelines}

| Command or rule | What it means or checks |
|---|---|
| Rule: `target: prerequisites` | Declares a Make target and the files it depends on |
| Make recipe line | Indented with a literal tab, never spaces (Pitfall above) |
| `make` | Rebuilds every target older than one of its prerequisites |
| `touch file` | Advances a file's timestamp without changing its contents; triggers Make, not `targets` |
| `tar_target(x, expr)` | Declares a `targets` target; the dependency graph is inferred from `expr` |
| `tar_target(x, path, format = 'file')` | Tracks `x` as a file, by content hash, not by R object |
| `tar_make()` | Builds every out-of-date target, in order, and skips the rest |
| `tar_outdated()` | Lists what a `tar_make()` would rebuild, without running anything |
| `tar_visnetwork()` | Draws the dependency graph, colored by up to date or out of date |
| `tar_render()` / `tar_quarto()` | Tracks a report's own source as well as the targets it reads |
| Capture vs. validation | A pipeline captures no determinant; it validates that an output is current |
| Honest claim | 'The pipeline re-executes reliably' is not 'the analysis is reproducible'; name the rung separately |
| LLM response cache | A committed file of model responses keyed by input hash, prompt version, and model identifier; the pipeline reads it and never queries (@sec-llm-in-pipeline) |

## Further reading

The definitive source on `targets` is its documentation
and the short paper that introduces it, @landau2021. That
paper states the 'function-oriented, Make-like' design
directly and is the natural starting point for an R
analyst. Its predecessor @landau2018 documents `drake`,
which a reader will still meet in existing projects and
which shares the same conceptual model. The manual-steps
critique that motivates the whole chapter is put crisply
by @sandve2013. Their rules on automating the path from
raw data to result are the pipeline idea stated as a rule
of conduct. For the language-agnostic and large-scale
tools, @koster2012 introduces Snakemake and @ditommaso2017
introduces Nextflow. Both repay reading by anyone whose
work will move into bioinformatics or onto a cluster. The
`workflowr` approach to binding rendered results to
version-control commits is described in @blischak2019. GNU
Make itself is documented in its own extensive manual. A
reader will consult it for the pattern rules and automatic
variables that this chapter's minimal treatment omitted.
For data-analysis uses specifically, the broader
software-carpentry literature on reproducible workflows,
of a piece with @wilson2014 and @wilson2017, situates Make
in the analyst's toolkit rather than the programmer's.
